archetype.name: Gunslinger (backup with a sneak package)
archetype.definition: A veteran who attacks downfield and accepts turnover risk when he starts, now the Giants' QB2 whose weekly role is a handful of designed short-yardage and goal-line runs.

report.headline: A competent fill-in starter, now a sneak specialist behind McCarthy
report.take:
Jameis Winston's 2026 has two parts. From Week 3 through Week 6 he was the Giants' starter and played like the Winston of the last decade: a 2-1-1 record, 7 touchdowns against 4 interceptions, and passing EPA per dropback of -0.03, which is roughly league-average quarterbacking with the usual mess around it. Since J.J. McCarthy took over in Week 7 he has been the QB2 with a specific job. He gets a few designed runs near the sticks and the goal line, plus one relief stint in Philadelphia where he went 6-of-8. His last three games he played 24%, 5% and 7% of snaps. That role, not his passing line, is what he is now.

The passing profile hasn't changed. His deep balls work: 24 throws of 20+ air yards produced +0.388 EPA a play on a 37.5% completion rate, which is the payoff for an aggressiveness rate near 21%. The 10-19 yard window is where he gets punished. All 5 of his interceptions came there, he completed 46.3%, and his bad-throw rate of 23.4% ranks 44th of 45. None of this is new. He led the league in yards and interceptions in 2019, and his 2025 bad-throw rate ranked dead last. The volatility comes with the arm. Sacks are the other steady leak: an 8.7% sack rate and 38.1% of pressures turned into sacks. Those are poor numbers for a quarterback whose 2.64-second time to throw isn't long.

The season totals also hide where the damage came from. His -12.7 passing EPA is weighed down by one relief appearance against the Rams in Week 2 (-12 EPA, 11-of-27), against a defense that now ranks 4th. His last start ended at 60% of snaps after a 14-of-26, two-interception day against the Saints, and the job changed hands the next week. The rushing line looks strange: 2.91 yards per carry with +0.623 EPA per carry. That is what a sneak package produces. His 14 designed runs averaged 1.21 yards, but 71.4% succeeded and two scored, because they are third-and-1s and goal-to-gos, not real carries.

Going forward, his value depends on McCarthy's availability and the Giants' willingness to keep using him in short yardage. The red-zone passing was sharp: 7 touchdowns on 19 attempts at +0.562 EPA a play. That would help if he were forced back in, but 19 throws is a hint, not a skill to bank on. As things stand, expect a few snaps a week, a carry or two near the stripe, and the occasional touchdown that swings a box score.

strengths.title: Short-yardage and goal-line runner
strengths.body: His designed runs are sneaks and keepers in must-gain spots, and they convert. They succeed at a high rate despite gaining almost nothing per carry. At 231 pounds he is a natural for the role. The touchdowns in Weeks 7 and 11 came from it, so it should last as long as the coaches keep calling it.

strengths.title: The deep ball still pays
strengths.body: Throws of 20+ air yards were his most productive area by a distance, and his completion rate over expected there was positive when it was negative at every other depth. His career aDOT and aggressiveness have always sat around this level, so this is a real trait, not a blip. It is also what made his starts watchable.

strengths.title: Finishing drives in the red zone
strengths.body: Inside the 20 he threw 7 touchdowns on 19 attempts with a big positive CPOE. The size of the arm matters less in tight windows near the goal line than his willingness to throw into them. The sample is small, so this is more a sign of comfort than a rate to project.

concerns.title: Intermediate interceptions and bad throws
concerns.body: Every interception came on 10-19 yard throws, where his accuracy falls off and he forces balls into zone windows. His bad-throw rate is near the bottom of the league. This matches his career, including a 30-interception 2019 and a last-place bad-throw rate in 2025. It is who he is and will not regress away.

concerns.title: Sacks and stalled third downs
concerns.body: Too many of his pressures became sacks. His third downs converted under a third of the time, partly because the average distance to go was nearly ten yards. His sack rate was worse than the league average, and drives died there. This is a recurring flaw, not something forced on him by the line: his time to throw is quick enough.

concerns.title: The role caps everything
concerns.body: He is QB2 and has played a sliver of the snaps in most games since Week 7, so his weekly output depends on a few package calls. The good recent efficiency numbers come from 9 dropbacks and mean little.

trend.note: He started Weeks 3-6, peaking with 326 yards and three touchdowns at Washington. After a two-interception loss to New Orleans in which he played only 60% of snaps, McCarthy took over. Since then his snap share has been in single digits apart from one relief outing.

nextGame.headline: Giants favored at Indy; his snaps hinge on short-yardage calls
nextGame.body:
The Book has the Giants as 6.5-point favorites with a 41.5 total, against a Colts offense that ranks last in passing EPA. That points to a game the Giants control on the ground, and Indianapolis is 28th in run-defense EPA and has given lead backs the most fantasy points over their averages in the league. A controlled, run-heavy script with red-zone trips is the best case for his package role: third-and-short and goal-to-go snaps are where he gets carries. If he were somehow pressed into passing duty, the setup would suit his arm. The Colts allow explosive passes at the 29th-ranked rate and are playing without both starting corners.

Availability matters mostly on the Indianapolis side. Charvarius Ward and Sauce Gardner, both regulars at 87% of snaps, are out, and so are starting tackles Jalen Travis and Bernhard Raimann. That further weakens a Colts offense that already struggles to move the ball, which helps the Giants keep a lead. On the Giants side, Tyrone Tracy Jr. is on IR with a projected December 6 return, so it does not change this week. Nothing in the dossier suggests McCarthy is limited, so Winston should be in his QB2 role.

keyMatchups.title: Sneak package vs a soft run defense
keyMatchups.body: Indianapolis struggles to stop the run and the Giants are favored. That should produce short-yardage and goal-line chances, which are the only snaps that reliably go to Winston now. Whether he gets one or two of them decides his day.

keyMatchups.title: Depleted Colts secondary if he throws
keyMatchups.body: With Gardner and Ward out and an explosive pass rate allowed near the bottom of the league, Indy is a matchup for vertical throws. That matters only if he enters in relief, but it is the scenario where his deep-ball strength shows.

keyMatchups.title: Game script as a favorite
keyMatchups.body: The Giants are 6.5-point favorites against an offense that ranks 31st in EPA, so they should be playing with a lead. A lead means more runs and more red-zone trips. It also means fewer reasons for any passing-package snaps.

nextGame.watch: Whether the Giants call his number on the first third-and-1 or goal-to-go, which shows if the package is still active.

restOfSeason.body:
As long as McCarthy starts, Winston is a role player whose production comes in small, lumpy pieces. He'll get a couple of designed carries most weeks, an occasional rushing touchdown, and rarely a pass. The rushing touchdowns are the swing: two scores on so few carries is a high rate that won't hold every week, so expect plenty of 1-3 point games mixed with 6-7 point games when he punches one in. Something like 1 to 7 PPR points a game, with 0 to 6 pass attempts, covers the typical range.

If he returns to the starting lineup, expect what he showed in Weeks 3-6. He should land around league-average efficiency, with deep-ball upside, intermediate interceptions and too many sacks, which means roughly 200-plus yards and close to two touchdowns a game with turnover risk. His red-zone passing efficiency is the piece most likely to cool. The interceptions and bad throws are the piece least likely to improve, because they have followed him for eleven seasons.
swingFactors: Whether the short-yardage package keeps getting called

confidence.note: The QB2 role is clear, but his weekly output rests on a few package snaps, and his recent passing comes from only 9 dropbacks.
